gaps.text: In-line measurement of Temperature at the measurement point with temperature sensor

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Fusion level: one model per method first, then a low-level fusion of block-scaled UV-Vis and Raman spectra. Both probes must sample the same small area and the two data streams must be normalised to a common time step. Each block keeps its own calibration, and the fused model must beat the best single method on held-out runs or the Raman block is dropped.)

items.finding: The source says that temperature sensitivity of OH bands in aqueous solution in NIR and MIR is a severe drawback, making tempered sample holders necessary.
items.how_it_applies: For in-line measurement in yeast fermentation, this suggests temperature at the measurement point may need to be controlled or monitored to reduce spectral variability; test with a temperature sensor or tempered holder.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement concerns NIR and MIR, not UV-Vis transmission/ATR, and aqueous solutions rather than fermentation broth; it is a review, not an in-line yeast study.

citation.quote: Additionally, the temperature sensitivity of the OH bands is a severe drawback for measuring aqueous solution in NIR and MIR, which makes tempered sample holders necessary [29].
citation.label: E03 ¶12

items.finding: Low-level data fusion is described as the simplest way to combine inputs by rearranging variables from different sources into a new data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This matches the proposed low-level fusion of block-scaled UV-Vis and Raman spectra; test whether concatenating variables improves over single methods.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: General PAT review, not yeast fermentation or UV-Vis/Raman specifically; no guidance on block scaling or time normalization.

citation.quote: Low-level data fusion (LLDF) is considered the simplest method to achieve a combination of inputs. In this case, the data is rearranged into a new data matrix, where the variables coming from different sources are placed one after the other.
citation.label: E01 ¶31

items.finding: The source notes that instrument complementarity was not sufficient to improve performance for several CQAs in a Raman and FT-IR food analytical study.
items.how_it_applies: This cautions that combining UV-Vis and Raman may not automatically beat the best single method; the fused model should be tested on held-out runs and the Raman block dropped if it does not add value.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited study used Raman and FT-IR on food, not UV-Vis and Raman on yeast fermentation; the result may not transfer to this matrix or process.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E01 ¶36

items.finding: Raman spectroscopy is frequently applied in upstream processing due to high selectivity and low water interference, despite relatively long measurement times.
items.how_it_applies: For in-line yeast fermentation, this suggests Raman may be selective for metabolites but measurement time could affect how early changes are detected; test time resolution.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The statement is about upstream processing generally, not yeast fermentation, and gives no detection limits or accuracy; it is a review.

citation.quote: Raman spectroscopy is frequently applied in upstream processing in research and industry due to its high selectivity and low water interference [55] despite the relatively long measurement times.
citation.label: E03 ¶20
